chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman, the freedman of Tribal, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).

Regarding a man who had sexual relations with his slave-girl, and that he used to send her on his errands, and that she became pregnant, and that news reached him of her promiscuity/mixing with others, so Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When she gives birth, he keeps the child and does not sell him, and assigns him a share in his house. He said: Then it was said to him, 'A man who has sexual relations with his slave-girl, and he did not send her on his errands, and he suspected her (of infidelity), and she became pregnant.' He said: When she gives birth, he keeps the child and does not sell him, and assigns him a share from his house and his wealth. This case is not like that other case.

The principle in these two narrations is that it was permissible for him not to fully affiliate the child to himself, such that his having relations with her was not simultaneous with another man's relations with her in the same period; rather, she was one of those whom he had relations with occasionally. So when another man had relations with her and the matter became mixed up, it was permissible for him not to fully affiliate the child to himself; rather, that is obligatory. He does not deny the child either, due to the suspicion in that case, and he sets aside for him something from his wealth, and does not make him share with the rest of his children and heirs who are of sound lineage. And this does not contradict that.

key_terms.فَسَاد: Promiscuity / Mixing with others (implying mixed paternity)

ai.seo_question: What are the inheritance and affiliation rules for a child born to a slave-girl from her master's lover?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfabar elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of *ilqâ'* (affiliation) in cases of *shubha* (ambiguity) where a master’s slave-girl bears a child by another man. It distinguishes between frequent and rare usage to determine the degree of paternity, ruling that the master retains the child and provides for him without selling him, yet excludes him from full inheritance shares to preserve the integrity of lineage (*ansab*). This reflects the Imami principle that paternity is not automatically negated by external conception but is modulated by the master's prior access and the resulting ambiguity.
